steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper comparing importance sampling methods (loss reweighting, undersampling, oversampling) for dealing with class imbalance in image classification, mainly on the Planet Rainforest satellite dataset. Motivate the problem, say what we test, and summarize what we found.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: detecting harmful activity in rainforests from satellite imagery
- Class imbalance / long-tail distributions and why they matter
- The Planet dataset as an example
- Theoretical angle and why not just get more data
- Importance sampling and the three methods we compare
- Experimental setup
- Summary of findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - detect illegal slash-and-burn + mining in protected rainforests; satellite imagery helps
  - satellite imagery covers vast areas -> lots of data to parse
  - classification models automate categorization of images by captured patterns
- Class imbalance
  - many large, widely-used datasets are long-tailed: some classes have far more examples (Figure 1)
  - models more accurate on overrepresented classes than underrepresented ones; like humans with more examples seen
  - induced bias -> dangerous, unfair predictions
- Planet Rainforest dataset
  - shows this trend; the detrimental activities users want to detect are among the worst-represented classes (Figure 1)
  - harder to remediate with multiple labels per image (as in Planet)
- Theory + more data
  - besides bounding generalization error on test sets, want empirical methods for minimizing expected error
  - understanding causes of poor generalization in practice -> intuition to constrain bounds
  - obvious fix: collect or generate more data; collecting is time-consuming + costly, generated data may not be realistic enough
  - better: leverage existing data
- Importance sampling
  - subset of methods recycling existing data to mitigate class imbalance
  - we compare: loss reweighting, undersampling, oversampling
- Setup
  - two datasets, different domains: Planet Rainforest, ADE20K
  - two image encoders: CLIP, ResNet-18
  - focus on Planet: varied, challenging tasks that accentuate class imbalance
  - ADE20K supplemental: completeness, generalizability
  - aim: datasets testing a skillset representative of broader model capabilities
- Findings
  - up-weighting loss on underrepresented classes: negligible effect, across both encoders
  - oversampling seems more effective than undersampling
  - undersampling could still be valuable with mindful (not random) selection
  - possible redundancy in Planet -> future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Detecting illegal slash-and-burn and mining activities in protected rainforests is crucial for the well-being of these areas, and satellite imagery can help with this. Satellite imagery covers vast areas, so there can be a large amount of data to go through. Classification models can speed this up by automatically categorizing the satellite images according to the patterns they capture.

However, many large and widely-used datasets have a long-tail distribution, where some classes have a lot more examples than others (Figure 1). Often machine learning models get higher accuracies on overrepresented classes than on underrepresented classes, in the same way a human would be better at classifying images from classes they have seen more examples of. But this induced bias can lead to dangerous and unfair model predictions.

We look at a satellite imagery dataset that shows this trend, the Planet Rainforest dataset. Actually the detrimental activities that users would want to detect are some of the worst-represented classes in the dataset (Figure 1). Also, this kind of distribution is harder to fix when each image has multiple labels, which is the case for the Planet dataset.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Detecting illegal slash-and-burn and mining activities in protected rainforests is crucial for the well-being of these areas, and satellite imagery can help with this. Satellite imagery covers vast areas, so there can be a large amount of data to go through. Classification models can speed this up by automatically categorizing the satellite images according to the patterns they capture.

However, many large and widely-used datasets have a long-tail distribution, where some classes have a lot more examples than others (Figure 1). Often machine learning models get higher accuracies on overrepresented classes than on underrepresented classes, in the same way a human would be better at classifying images from classes they have seen more examples of. But this induced bias can lead to dangerous and unfair model predictions.

We look at a satellite imagery dataset that shows this trend, the Planet Rainforest dataset. Actually the detrimental activities that users would want to detect are some of the worst-represented classes in the dataset (Figure 1). Also, this kind of distribution is harder to fix when each image has multiple labels, which is the case for the Planet dataset.

From a theoretical machine learning perspective, besides bounding generalization error when we evaluate models on test sets, we may also want to develop empirical methods for minimizing expected error. If we understand what causes poor generalization in practice, we can get intuition that helps to further constrain bounds when we develop models.

A natural solution to class imbalance would be to just collect or generate more data. But depending on the application, collecting data is often time-consuming and costly, and generating data may not give sufficiently realistic representations. In general it would be beneficial to find ways to use the data that already exists.

Importance sampling is a subset of methods that recycle existing data to mitigate the effects of class imbalance. So we explore and compare three importance sampling based methods: loss reweighting, undersampling, and oversampling.

We experiment with two datasets from different domains, the Planet Rainforest and the ADE20K datasets, and with two image encoders, CLIP and ResNet-18. We mostly focus on the Planet dataset, since we think it provides varied, challenging tasks that can accentuate the effects of class imbalance. But we also include some supplemental experiments on ADE20K, for completeness and to see how generalizable our findings are. We try to evaluate our findings on datasets that test a skillset that is representative of broader model capabilities.

For both types of encoders, we find that up-weighting the loss on underrepresented classes has a negligible effect on performance. We also find that oversampling seems to be more effective than undersampling. Still, our results suggest that undersampling could be a valuable method if the samples are selected mindfully instead of at random. Finally, our experiments indicate that there may be some redundancy in the Planet dataset, which motivates new avenues for future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Detecting illegal slash-and-burn and mining activities in protected rainforests is crucial for ensuring the well-being of such areas, and satellite imagery can facilitate this process. Because satellite imagery can cover vast areas, there can be a large amount of data to parse. Classification models can expedite this process by automating the categorization of satellite images according to their captured patterns.

However, many large and widely-used datasets exhibit a long-tail distribution, where some classes have significantly more examples than others (Figure 1) [1,2,3,4,5,6]. Machine learning models often achieve higher accuracies on overrepresented classes than on underrepresented classes, much as a human would be better at classifying images from classes for which they have seen more examples [7,8,9,10]. However, this induced bias can lead to dangerous and unfair model predictions [11,12,13,14].

We explore a satellite imagery dataset that demonstrates this trend, the Planet Rainforest dataset [15,16]. In fact, the detrimental activities that users would want to detect are among the worst-represented classes in the dataset (Figure 1). This type of distribution also becomes more difficult to remediate when each image has multiple labels, as is the case with the Planet dataset.

From a theoretical machine learning perspective, in addition to bounding generalization error when we evaluate models on test sets, we may also be interested in developing empirical methods for minimizing expected error. By understanding the causes of poor generalization in practice, we can gain intuition to further constrain bounds when developing models.

A natural solution to class imbalance would be to simply collect or generate more data. Depending on the application, however, collecting data is often time-consuming and costly, and generating data may not produce sufficiently realistic representations. In general, exploring ways to leverage existing data would be beneficial.

Importance sampling covers a subset of methods that recycle existing data to mitigate the effects of class imbalance [17,18,19,20,21]. We therefore explore and compare three importance sampling based methods: loss reweighting, undersampling, and oversampling.

Specifically, we experiment with two datasets from different domains, the Planet Rainforest [15,16] and the ADE20K [5] datasets, and with two image encoders, CLIP [22] and ResNet-18 [23]. We primarily focus on the Planet dataset, since we believe it provides varied, challenging tasks that can accentuate the effects of class imbalance. We also include supplemental experiments on ADE20K, for completeness and to observe how generalizable our findings are. We aim to evaluate our findings on datasets that test a skillset representative of broader model capabilities.

Across both types of encoders, we find that up-weighting the loss on underrepresented classes has a negligible effect on performance. We also find that oversampling appears to be more effective than undersampling. That said, our results suggest that undersampling could still be valuable if samples are selected mindfully rather than at random. Finally, our experiments indicate that there may be some redundancy in the Planet dataset, which motivates new avenues for future work.
